---
title: "Picking the right structure"
---

You built three containers by hand in this part, and every one of them holds
your songs just as happily as it holds the hairdresser's customers. That is what
makes the choice hard: nothing in TypeScript stops you from putting a waiting
line into a stack. You already made this choice four times in your own
projects, so this chapter starts by reading the reasons back out of your own
code.

## Four projects, four answers {#sec-choosing-experiment}

1. Open `homework/bracelet-tests` and find the field in `Bracelet` that holds
   the beads.

2. Open `coursework/playlist` and find the field in `Playlist` that holds the
   songs.

3. Open `homework/undo-counter` and find the fields inside `UndoStack`.

4. Open `coursework/hairdresser` and find the fields inside `WaitingLine`.

Four classes, four different answers. The bracelet keeps an array. The playlist
keeps one pointer to the first node. The undo stack keeps one pointer and a
counter. The waiting line keeps two pointers, one to each end.

None of those four is better than the others. Each one is the cheapest way to
do what its own app actually does, and you can say why in one sentence.
That sentence is the skill this chapter is about. When somebody asks why the
undo history is not an array, "because we did it that way in the book" is not
an answer you want to give.

## What each structure is good at {#sec-choosing-table}

Six containers are yours by now, and this table is the short version of what
each one is for. The reasons sit underneath it, because a table cell is too
small to argue in.

| Structure | Good at | Expensive or impossible | In this book |
|---|---|---|---|
| Array | Reaching item number 5 in one step, keeping a fixed order you loop over | Inserting or removing at the front, which shifts everything behind it | The aquarium's `private fishes: Fish[]` |
| Linked list | Inserting and removing wherever you already stand, growing without copying | Reaching item number 5, because you walk there node by node | The playlist |
| Stack | Handing back the newest item, over and over | Reaching anything but the top; there is no item number 5 | The undo history of the counter |
| Queue | Serving the oldest item, so nobody jumps the line | Reaching into the middle, same as the stack | The hairdresser's waiting line |
| `Map` | Finding a value by a key you already have | Anything you cannot phrase as a key, such as "which one is highlighted" | Paint's `Map<ToolType, HTMLButtonElement>` |
| `Set` | Answering "is this in here", and removing the value itself with no index | Positions and keys; a duplicate silently disappears | Paint's `Set<Shape>` |

The array is still the one you reach for first, and that is not laziness. An
array reaches item number 5 in a single step because the items sit next to each
other in memory, and the cost table in @sec-linked-list-costs put a price on
that layout: the front. Everything behind an inserted item moves one slot to
the right.

A linked list pays the opposite bill. Nothing shifts, because a node lives
wherever it happens to live and only the arrows change, so inserting is a
couple of assignments no matter how long the chain is. What you give up is the
index. Song number 5 costs five steps, song number 500 costs 500, and every
`length` that walks the chain costs the same again.

A stack and a queue are linked lists with a rule attached, and the rule is the
whole point. `Stack<T>` has no method that reaches into the middle, so a bug
cannot take the wrong action back. `WaitingLine<T>` serves the head and appends
at the tail, so nobody jumps the line even when you are careless. Choosing one
of these two tells the next reader of your code something no comment can
promise: this collection is only ever touched at one end.

`Map` and `Set` are not about order at all. They are about the question you
ask. Paint keeps its buttons in a `Map` because a button has a name you look it
up by, and it keeps its shapes in a `Set` because a shape has no name and gets
deleted as itself, with no index to find first.

::: {.callout-tip}
## You will still write push and pop on an array

In a real project you would not hand-write a stack. `push` and `pop` on a
plain array are cheap, because both happen at the end, where nothing has to
shift. A queue on an array is the one that hurts: `shift` takes the first item
and moves every other item one slot left, so a long queue pays on every single
`dequeue`.

The hand-built versions still bought you two things. You can now read code that
walks a chain of nodes, which is most of what a data structures course anywhere
looks like, and you know what `push` costs instead of guessing. The exam wants
the hand-built version, and your future job wants the array. Both are fine, as
long as you know which one you are looking at.
:::

## Two questions to ask before you write the class {#sec-choosing-questions}

Naming a structure is the last step, not the first. Two questions get you there
almost every time, and both of them are about what the app does rather than
about what TypeScript offers.

**Where do items go in and come out?** In and out at the same end is a stack.
In at one end and out at the other is a queue. A lot of coming and going in the
middle is a linked list. Any position you can count to is an array.

**How do you find one again?** By its position is an array. By a key you
already hold is a `Map`. By nothing more than "is it in there at all" is a
`Set`. By walking until something matches is a linked list, and if you catch
yourself doing that on every click, the second question just told you to switch
to a `Map`.

Sometimes both answers are "neither", and the honest choice is no collection at
all. The bracelet remembers whether it has already shown the color warning with
a single boolean field, not with a list of warnings it has given. The bank
account holds one private number. A structure you do not need is a structure
that can go out of sync with the thing it is supposed to describe.

## Exercise: pick one {#sec-choosing-exercise}

Two apps, and you build exactly one of them. The browser history needs two
stacks working against each other. The print queue needs one queue and a form.
Read both, then pick the one whose structure you can already explain out loud.

Both of them start by copying a class you wrote earlier in this part, tests
included. That is the payoff for having kept the logic out of `index.ts` since
Part 5.

### Option A: the browser history {#sec-choosing-history}

{{< exercise browser-history tests=true title="Files for the browser history" >}}

1. Create a new app from our tests template inside `coursework/`, in a folder
   called `browser-history`. Delete `src/math.ts` and `src/math.test.ts`, and
   cut `src/index.ts` down to one line, `import './styles.css';`.

2. Copy `src/stack.ts` and `src/stack.test.ts` out of `coursework/train-builder`
   into this project's `src/` folder and run `npm test`. Every test that was
   green in the train builder is green here, and you changed nothing: a tested
   class in its own file is the thing you get to carry from app to app.

3. Write `src/browser-history.ts` test first, in the rhythm you know by now.
   One `it`, watch it fail, make it pass. `BrowserHistory` keeps two
   `Stack<string>` fields and a `currentPage: string | null`, and it offers
   `visit(page)`,
   `back()`, `forward()`, and the getters `current`, `canGoBack`, and
   `canGoForward`. Four sentences to write as tests:

   * a fresh history has no current page, and it can go neither back nor
     forward
   * after visiting two pages, `back()` puts the first page back on screen and
     Forward becomes possible
   * calling `forward()` right after that `back()` returns to the second page
   * visiting a new page after a `back()` throws the forward pages away

   The rules behind those four: `visit` pushes the page you are leaving onto
   the back stack and then replaces the forward stack with a fresh one, `back`
   pops the back stack and pushes the page you are leaving onto the forward
   stack, and `forward` is the same two lines with the stacks swapped. Your
   `Stack<T>` has no `clear`, so throwing the forward history away is
   `this.forwardStack = new Stack<string>();`.

4. Wire `src/index.ts`. Look up the form, the address input, the two buttons,
   and the `<output>`, and stop the app with one `if` and a `throw` when any of
   them is missing. Keep one `const pageHistory = new BrowserHistory();` next
   to them. Write a `render()` that puts `pageHistory.current` into the output,
   shows `nothing yet` while there is none, and disables each button when its
   getter says `false`. The form's `submit` listener calls `preventDefault()`,
   visits what the user typed, empties the input, and renders. Call `render()`
   once at the end of the file.

5. Run `npm start` and walk through it. Expected results:

   * the fresh page shows `nothing yet` with both buttons gray
   * after `news.example`, Back is still gray, because there is nowhere to go
     back to
   * after `sports.example` and then `weather.example`, Back is active and
     Forward is gray
   * Back twice shows `sports.example`, then `news.example`, with Back gray
     again and Forward active
   * Forward once returns to `sports.example`
   * typing `maps.example` and pressing Go turns Forward gray again, because a
     new visit throws the forward history away

6. Add the `verify` script to `package.json` as in every new app, run
   `npm run verify`, fix what it reports, and commit.

### Option B: the print queue {#sec-choosing-printer}

{{< exercise print-queue tests=true title="Files for the print queue" >}}

1. Create a new app from our tests template inside `coursework/`, in a folder
   called `print-queue`. Delete `src/math.ts` and `src/math.test.ts`, and cut
   `src/index.ts` down to one line, `import './styles.css';`.

2. Copy `src/waiting-line.ts` and `src/waiting-line.test.ts` out of
   `coursework/hairdresser` into this project's `src/` folder and run
   `npm test`. Everything is green here too, because `T` never mentioned a
   customer.

3. Create `src/print-job.ts` with one type:

   ```ts
   export type PrintJob = {
     documentName: string;
     pages: number;
   };
   ```

   Then write `src/print-job.test.ts` with a single `it`: a
   `new WaitingLine<PrintJob>()` that got two jobs hands back the one added
   first, and its `length` is 1 afterwards. This test is green the moment you
   save it, and that is exactly what it is there to prove. The queue you wrote
   for people at a hairdresser works for print jobs without a single edit.

4. Wire `src/index.ts`. Look up the form, both inputs, the Print next button,
   the `<output>`, the `<ol>`, and the message paragraph in one `if`, and keep
   one `const jobs = new WaitingLine<PrintJob>();` next to them. The `submit`
   listener calls `preventDefault()`, enqueues a job built from the two inputs,
   and clears the document name. The Print next listener dequeues, leaves right
   away when the answer is `null`, writes the job into the output, and renders.
   `render()` does three things:

   * empty the list with `replaceChildren()` and add one `<li>` per entry of
     `jobs.toArray()`, each showing the document name and its page count
   * disable Print next while `jobs.isEmpty()`
   * write `Nothing is waiting.` into the message paragraph, or the number of
     jobs that are

   Watch your plural in both places. One page is `1 page` and three are
   `3 pages`, one job is `1 job waiting` and two are `2 jobs waiting`.

5. Both inputs sit inside a `<form>` on this page, so `required`, `min="1"`,
   and `step="1"` do more work than they did for the counter's Add button: the
   browser checks them before it fires `submit`. Run `npm start`. Expected
   results:

   * the fresh page shows `Printing: nothing`, an empty list, `Nothing is
     waiting.`, and a gray Print next
   * add `essay.txt` with 3 pages and then `photo.png` with 1 page: two lines
     in that order, `2 jobs waiting`, and Print next active
   * Print next shows `essay.txt (3 pages)`, drops it from the list, and leaves
     `1 job waiting`, because the job that waited longest goes first
   * Print next again shows `photo.png (1 page)`, empties the list, and turns
     itself gray
   * typing `2.5` into Pages and pressing Add job gets you the browser's own
     complaint, and nothing joins the queue

6. Add the `verify` script to `package.json` as in every new app, run
   `npm run verify`, fix what it reports, and commit.

::: {.callout-tip}
## When you finish early

**Show the stacks.** In the browser history, put two `<ul>` elements on the
page and fill them from `toArray()` on each stack, so you can watch a page name
move from one stack to the other when you press Back. `toArray()` hands you the
top first, which is the order Back would visit them in.

**Cancel a job.** In the print queue, put a Cancel button next to every waiting
job, and try to make it work. `WaitingLine<T>` only ever removes at the head,
so canceling the third job is not something its methods can do. Decide what to
change: a `delete` that walks the chain and unhooks one node, the way the
playlist does it, or a different structure entirely. Whichever you pick, you
just did the thing this chapter is about.
:::
